'''John P. Ferraris''' (April 1947 – May 2025) was an American chemist and professor at the [[University of Texas at Dallas]]. He was known for his pioneering work in the field of [[organic electronics]], particularly the discovery that a [[charge-transfer complex]] between [[tetrathiafulvalene]] (TTF) and [[tetracyanoquinodimethane]] (TCNQ) exhibits high electrical conductivity.<ref name="TTF-TCNQ1973">Ferraris, J. P.; Cowan, D. O.; Walatka, V.; Perlstein, J. H. (1973). "Electron transfer in a new highly conducting donor-acceptor complex". ''Journal of the American Chemical Society''. '''95''' (3): 948–949. doi:[10.1021/ja00784a066](https://doi.org/10.1021/ja00784a066).</ref> This finding helped establish the foundation for the development of [[conducting polymers]] and organic electronic materials.

== Early life and education ==
Ferraris earned his B.A. in chemistry from [[Saint Michael's College]] in [[Vermont]] in 1969.<ref name="UTDProfile">[https://profiles.utdallas.edu/john.ferraris John P. Ferraris Faculty Profile]. University of Texas at Dallas. Accessed May 2025.</ref> He then completed both an M.A. (1971) and a Ph.D. (1974) in organic chemistry at [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref name="UTDProfile" /> While a graduate student, he co-authored a seminal paper demonstrating high conductivity in a 1:1 charge-transfer salt of TTF and TCNQ, marking a significant advance in the field of [[organic conductor]]s.<ref name="TTF-TCNQ1973" />

Following his doctoral studies, Ferraris was a National Research Council postdoctoral fellow at the National Bureau of Standards (now NIST) from 1973 to 1975.<ref name="NanoTechProfile">Ferraris, J. P., Curriculum Vitae (Archived UT Dallas NanoTech Institute, 2017).</ref>

== Career ==
Ferraris joined the chemistry faculty at the [[University of Texas at Dallas]] in 1975.<ref name="UTDProfile" /> He became a full professor in 1992 and served as head of the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry from 1995 to 2017.<ref name="NanoTechProfile" /> Between 2003 and 2006, he was Interim Dean of the School of Natural Sciences and Mathematics. From 2006 to 2009, he held the Cecil H. and Ida Green Chair in [[Systems biology|Systems Biology]] Science.<ref name="UTDProfile" />

He has authored over 150 publications and holds numerous U.S. patents.<ref name="UTDProfile" /> Ferraris has collaborated on interdisciplinary research in electroactive polymers, nanomaterials, [[gas separation]] membranes, and artificial muscles. He played a key role in the UT Dallas [[NanoTech Institute]], working alongside [[Alan MacDiarmid]], [[Ray Baughman]], and [[Anvar Zakhidov]].<ref name="Science2006">Ebron, V. H.; Yang, Z.; Seyer, D. S.; et al. (2006). "Fuel powered artificial muscles". ''Science''. '''311''' (5767): 1580–1583. doi:[10.1126/science.1121401](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1121401).</ref>

== Research Contributions ==
=== Organic Conductors ===
Ferraris co-authored the 1973 paper reporting high conductivity in the TTF-TCNQ charge-transfer complex.<ref name="TTF-TCNQ1973" /> This was the first demonstration of metallic-like conductivity in an organic material and laid the foundation for the field of organic metals and conducting polymers.

=== Conducting Polymers and Energy Materials ===
He developed low bandgap conjugated polymers for use in optoelectronic devices and contributed to the design of conductive membranes and polymer-based supercapacitors.<ref name="Electrochimica2000">Yue, X.; Balkus, K. J.; Ferraris, J. P. (2000). "Novel proton conducting polymer electrolyte membranes for fuel cells". ''Electrochimica Acta''. '''45''' (25–26): 4211–4217. doi:[10.1016/S0013-4686(00)00549-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0013-4686(00)00549-4).</ref>

=== Nanotechnology and Devices ===
Ferraris co-developed super-tough [[carbon nanotube]] fibers<ref name="Nature2003">Dalton, A. B.; Collins, S.; Munoz, E.; et al. (2003). "Super-tough carbon-nanotube fibres". ''Nature''. '''423''' (6941): 703. doi:[10.1038/423703a](https://doi.org/10.1038/423703a).</ref> and co-invented chemically powered artificial muscles.<ref name="Science2006" />

== Awards and honors ==
* '''W.T. Doherty Award''' (2001), from the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Dallas–Fort Worth Section.<ref name="DohertyAward">[https://dfwacs.org/Doherty_Award Doherty Award Past Recipients]. Dallas–Fort Worth ACS Section.</ref>
* '''Cecil H. and Ida Green Chair in Systems Biology Science''', held from 2006 to 2009.<ref name="UTDProfile" />
